title: The Young Man Who Could Not Stay Silent
sum: The three friends have given up. Job has sworn his innocence (chapter 31), and no one answers. Then a new man steps forward: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, young, angry, and never mentioned before. The narrator tells us four times that his anger blazed: at Job, for making himself right rather than God, and at the friends, for condemning Job without answering him.

Elihu apologizes for his youth and then sets it aside. Wisdom, he says, does not come with gray hair but from the spirit God breathes into a person. He has waited and listened, and he is so full of words that he will burst like a wineskin. He promises to flatter no one. Whether he is a prophet, a windbag, or both, is a question every reader of Job has to answer.
readings: Read as a forerunner

Elihu is the human voice that prepares for God's. He rejects the friends' failed answers, offers a new one (suffering as warning and teaching), and ends by describing the storm out of which God speaks (37:1–5; 38:1). His claim to the spirit (32:8, 18) is the claim of a prophet.
Read as comedy

Elihu is a young man swollen with his own importance. He announces at length that he is about to speak (32:6–22), compares himself to a bursting wineskin, and promises fresh answers that turn out to repeat the friends. The book lets him talk and then ignores him: God never mentions him.
Read as a later addition

Elihu is missing from the prologue and from the verdict on the friends (42:7–9), and his Hebrew has its own flavor. On this view a later writer, unhappy with the dialogue, added a voice that defends God more strongly and better prepares for the divine speeches.

views.H: Readers who take Job as history see Elihu as another man of the East, a relative of Abraham's clan through Buz (Genesis 22:21), who was present at the debate and spoke last because he was youngest. His absence from 42:7–9 is explained as God passing over him because he spoke better than the friends, or because his words are answered by God's own.
views.C: Many critical scholars (Driver and Gray, Pope, Dhorme) think chapters 32–37 were added by a later writer: Elihu is introduced in prose that does not match the prologue, he quotes Job like someone reading a finished text, his vocabulary differs, and 38:1 follows 31:40 smoothly. Others (Gordis, Habel, Hartley) argue that the same author wrote them, perhaps later in life, and that the book's design needs a human answer before the divine one.
views.W: Ancient wisdom texts also stage debates with several speakers. The Babylonian Theodicy is a dialogue of a sufferer and a friend, and in Ludlul bel nemeqi the sufferer is rescued after dreams in which messengers appear. Elihu's appeal to inspiration over age turns the usual wisdom rule, that the old speak first, upside down.
views.J: The Talmud counts Elihu among seven prophets who prophesied to the nations: Balaam and his father, Job, Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar and Elihu (Bava Batra 15b), and asks whether Elihu, "of the clan of Ram," was in fact an Israelite. Medieval commentators such as Gersonides (Ralbag) and Nachmanides valued Elihu's speeches highly as the closest a human comes to the truth in the book. By contrast, the Testament of Job, a Jewish work in Greek that is in no Bible today, makes Elihu a speaker inspired by Satan whom God does not forgive.
views.X: Gregory the Great read Elihu as a picture of proud believers who say true things arrogantly. Thomas Aquinas judged that Elihu came nearer the truth than the friends but was wrong to accuse Job of hidden sin. Calvin preached many sermons on Elihu and treated much of his teaching as sound. Some Christian readers see him as a forerunner like John the Baptist, announcing the One who comes after him.

deep.b:
1. A later addition. The case: Elihu is not named in the prologue, in the narrator's list of visitors (2:11), or in the LORD's verdict on the friends (42:7–9). His speeches have their own words (de'a for "knowledge," more Aramaic forms, a liking for El as God's name), he quotes Job's earlier speeches like someone with the text in front of him (33:9–11; 34:5–6), and the LORD's first words in 38:1–2 read most naturally as an answer to Job's last words in 31:35–37. Scholars such as Driver and Gray and Marvin Pope hold this view. Against it: every manuscript and ancient translation has the speeches in this place, and a later writer could have been the same poet returning to his work.

2. A pompous young man whom the book mocks. The narrator stresses his anger four times; he spends a whole chapter announcing that he will speak; he compares himself to a bursting wineskin full of "wind" (32:18–19); he calls himself "complete in knowledge" (36:4), a phrase he later uses of God (37:16). William Whedbee and others read him as comic relief, and Norman Habel as a self-appointed arbiter whose claims the book quietly undercuts. God's silence about him is the final joke.

3. A true forerunner of God's speeches. Elihu says things the friends never said: God speaks through dreams and through pain to turn a person back (33:14–30); suffering can be discipline and warning, not only punishment (36:8–15); a heavenly go-between may plead for the sufferer (33:23–24). His last speech turns to God's power in the rain, thunder and snow (36:27–37:13), asks Job "Do you know...?" as God will (37:14–18), and describes the storm out of which God speaks (37:1–5; 38:1). God does not rebuke him, perhaps because he was right enough. Hartley, Andersen, many medieval Jewish commentators and Calvin lean this way.

4. A prophet (Jewish tradition). The Talmud names him among seven prophets sent to the nations of the world (Bava Batra 15b), taking his claim to the spirit (32:8, 18; 33:4) at face value.

5. A mediator figure (Christian readings). Christian readers have heard in the mal'akh melits, "angel, go-between" (33:23), and the "ransom" (33:24) a picture of Christ, the one mediator who gives himself as a ransom (1 Timothy 2:5–6). Some go further and see Elihu himself, who says he stands for Job before God (33:6), as a forerunner of that mediator.

The Hebrew text of chapters 32–37 is well preserved but very difficult, with many rare words (see 34:29–33; 36:16–20; 36:33). The Old Greek translation of Job is about a sixth shorter than the Hebrew, and scholars who have studied the gaps report that they grow larger in the later chapters, including Elihu's. Origen filled the gaps from the later Greek version of Theodotion and marked them with asterisks; Later manuscripts such as Codex Vaticanus print the filled-out text, with a few lines missing (35:3 is one), and without Origen's signs, so a Greek line in Vaticanus may be Theodotion's rather than the Old Greek (see Peter Gentry's study of the asterisked lines).

In Elihu's speeches the Old Greek lacked, among others: most of 32:11–17 (in their place it starts a second speech, "And Elihu went on and said"); 33:28–29 and 33:32–33; 35:3, 35:7b–10a and 35:15–16; most of 36:5–11, 36:20b–21 and 36:24b–28; nearly all of 36:29–37:5; and parts of 34:25–33 and 37:6–17. This list follows the asterisks in Jerome's Latin translation of Origen's Greek, which the editors warn are not always reliable; the Göttingen edition may mark the edges differently.

What was checked. The Greek was checked in Tischendorf's edition (the Sixtine text of 1587, based on Codex Vaticanus) and Origen's signs in Jerome's hexaplaric Latin Job (Patrologia Latina 29). The book method names Rahlfs's edition and NETS, but neither could be reached for this part. The Qumran witnesses were not checked: 4QJob-a preserves parts of 32:3–4, 33:10–11 and 24–30, 35:16, 36:7–11, 13–27 and 32–33, and 37:1–5 and 14–15; 2QJob preserves parts of 33:28–30; and the Aramaic Targum 11QtgJob covers much of 32–37. The Syriac was not checked either; where I mention the Vulgate or the rabbinic Targum, I rely on the standard commentaries.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Elihu is the reader's own voice
deep.b: Elihu arrives after the reader has heard the whole debate, and he says what many readers feel at that point: someone has to defend God, and the friends did it badly. He quotes Job's words back like someone who has the text open (33:9–11; 34:5–6), he speaks to Job, to the friends and to an audience of "wise men" (34:2), and he sums up with the verdict a reader might write in the margin: "Job talks without knowing" (34:35). My suggestion is that the book gives this reaction the best voice it can, lets it reach its strongest point (the storm hymn), and then has God speak past it without comment. The silence in 42:7–9 is the book's answer: even a better defense of God is still a human defense. This overlaps with Carol Newsom's reading of Elihu as a "dissenting reader" of the dialogue; the stress on the reader's own reaction is mine.

echoes: Genesis 2:7; Genesis 22:21; Jeremiah 25:23; Jeremiah 20:9; Amos 3:8; Matthew 9:17; 1 Samuel 1:1; 12:12; 15:2; 15:10; 42:7–9

settings.when: after Job's oath (chapter 31) and the friends' silence
settings.why: To bring in a new speaker no one expected, and to tell us how to hear him: young, waiting his turn, and four times angry, at Job for justifying himself and at the friends for condemning Job without answering him.
settings.readers: For Israelites asking why the faithful suffer, the narrator signals that the friends' answers have failed and that a new kind of answer is coming. Whether Elihu gives it, or only prepares for God's, is left for the reader to decide.

settings.what: Elihu's opening: why the young may speak
settings.by: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite
settings.to: First the three friends ("you" plural, "you are gray-haired," 32:6–14), then the onlookers or himself, speaking of the friends as "they" (32:15–22)
settings.when: as the friends fall silent, before he turns to Job
settings.why: To claim the right to speak despite his age (wisdom is from God's spirit, not years), to rebuke the friends for failing to refute Job, and to promise an answer free of flattery and favoritism.
settings.readers: Readers in a community that honored elders would feel the shock of a young man correcting them. The book tests the claim that inspiration outranks experience by letting Elihu speak at length and then judging his words by God's.
views: To the friends and an audience
Elihu speaks to the friends, then turns to bystanders who have watched the debate, the same "wise men" of 34:2.
32:15–22 may be Elihu talking to himself, a stage aside that shows how full of words he is.

title: God Speaks Twice
sum: Elihu turns to Job and calls him by name, which the friends never did. He offers himself as an equal, made of the same clay, so Job need not fear him. Then he quotes Job: I am pure, yet God treats me as an enemy. Elihu's reply is the heart of his first speech. Job says God does not answer, but God speaks, once and twice, even when no one notices.

God speaks first in dreams, warning a person away from pride. He speaks second through pain, when a sick man's flesh wastes away and he draws near the Pit. Then, if an angel, a go-between, one in a thousand, speaks for him, God says, "Spare him; I have found a ransom." The man is healed, prays, sees God's face with joy, and sings of his rescue. God does this two times, three times, to bring a person back to the light.
readings: Read as a new answer
Elihu goes beyond the friends: suffering is not only payback for sin but God's way of speaking, a warning meant to save. It gives pain a purpose without proving the sufferer wicked.
Read as the old answer in new clothes

The dying man still has to confess his sin (33:27), so Elihu still assumes that Job's suffering points to wrongdoing. The reader, who knows the scene in heaven (1:6–12), knows that is not why Job suffers.

views.H: Readers who take the scene as history hear Elihu teaching Job a real path back to God, one Job in a sense follows in 42:1–6, though God, not Elihu, is the one who brings him there.
views.C: Critical scholars note how closely Elihu quotes Job (33:9–11 from 13:24, 27) and Eliphaz (33:15 from 4:13), evidence for some that the Elihu speeches were written by someone reading the finished dialogue. The text of 33:16–28 has several hard spots and a Ketiv/Qere pair in 33:28.
views.W: The Babylonian poem Ludlul bel nemeqi tells of a sufferer brought near death and then rescued after dreams in which divine messengers come to him. The Hebrew verb for being "nipped off" from clay (33:6) is the one Akkadian poems use for the making of humans. Elihu's go-between resembles the personal gods of Mesopotamia who plead for their worshiper.
views.J: The Talmud reads 33:23 as an angel advocate: even if 999 argue against a person and one argues for him, he is saved (Shabbat 32a). From 33:29 it learns that God forgives a repeated sin up to three times (Yoma 86b). Maimonides says the angel's intercession is the one idea Elihu adds to the friends' (Guide 3.23), and Nachmanides found a hint of the soul's return in 33:29–30.
views.X: Christians have long seen in the go-between and the ransom (33:23–24) a picture of Christ, the one mediator between God and humans, who gave himself as a ransom (1 Timothy 2:5–6; Mark 10:45). Others read the verse of guardian angels, or of preachers who show sinners the right way. See "Where Christians differ."

deep.b:
An angel in God's court. Most Jewish and modern readers take the mal'akh melits as an angel who speaks for the dying man, the opposite of the Accuser of chapters 1–2 and of the "death-dealers" in 33:22. Eliphaz had doubted that any of "the holy ones" would answer Job (5:1); Elihu says one might. The Targum makes him "one advocate among a thousand accusers."

A human messenger. Mal'akh often means a human messenger, and melits an interpreter (Genesis 42:23). On this reading the go-between is a prophet or wise teacher who shows the sufferer what is right (33:23), perhaps Elihu himself, who has just said he stands before God as Job's equal (33:6).

Christ. Christian readers from the early church on have seen here the one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5) who pleads for sinners (Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1) and gives his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45). Most who hold this view treat it as a fuller meaning that Elihu could not have seen, not as his own intention.

Job's own hope. Whatever the go-between is, Elihu's words answer Job's longings for an umpire (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19–21) and a redeemer (19:25). The reader is left to decide whether Elihu has understood Job's hope or turned it into something smaller.

Eliphaz said God's correction is a blessing (5:17–18), so Elihu's idea is not wholly new. What is new is the order and the purpose. For the friends, suffering shows that a person has sinned. For Elihu, suffering is a message sent before a person is lost, to turn him back (33:17–18, 30). His picture also includes an advocate, a ransom and a public song of thanks, none of which the friends mention. Fair readers grant him this advance. They also note its limit: Elihu still expects Job to confess sin (33:27), while the reader knows from the prologue that Job's suffering began as a test of his integrity (1:8–12; 2:3).

traditions.q: Does the angel and go-between of Job 33:23–24 show that angels plead for people before God, or does it point to Christ alone?
views: Angels truly watch over and intercede for every human life from beginning to death (Catechism 336), so a literal angelic advocate fits Catholic teaching; Catholic interpreters also read the verse spiritually of Christ, the one Mediator in whom all other help shares.

The Orthodox Church honors each person's guardian angel and asks the angels' prayers in its services, for example in the Canon of Supplication to the Guardian Angel, which asks the angel to intercede for the sinner before God. So it can read the verse of an angel who pleads for the sinner, while confessing Christ as the one who gives his life as the ransom.

The Lutheran Confessions grant that angels pray for us, but they reject calling on angels or saints as mediators, because Scripture sets forth Christ alone as Mediator and atoning sacrifice (Apology of the Augsburg Confession, article 21). The "ransom" is read in the light of Christ.

Christ is the only Mediator between God and humans (Westminster Confession 8), and worship and prayer go to God alone, not to angels (21.2). Reformed preachers apply the go-between to Christ, or to the faithful minister who declares God's righteousness to sinners, not to an angel who pleads in heaven.

settings.what: Elihu's first speech to Job: God speaks in dreams and in pain
settings.when: after his opening words to the friends; Job sits in his illness and does not reply
settings.why: To answer Job's complaint that God will not respond (33:13) by arguing that God speaks in warning dreams and through sickness, and to offer Job a way back: hear the warning, confess, pray, and be restored.
settings.readers: For Israelites who read suffering, even the exile if the book is from after it, as many think, as God's discipline, Elihu's picture of pain as a warning that can end in rescue and praise was familiar from the psalms. The book sets it beside Job's case to test whether it explains every kind of suffering.

title: Far Be It from God
sum: Elihu now speaks to a wider circle: "you wise men," "you who know." He invites them to judge Job's words with him, as the ear tests words and the mouth tastes food. He quotes Job: I am righteous, and God has taken away my rights. Is there anyone like Job, who drinks scorn like water?

His answer is one claim, argued from every side: God would never do wrong. A God who made the world and keeps every creature breathing cannot be unjust; a ruler who hated justice could not rule at all. God shows no favor to princes over the poor, sees every step people take, and brings down the mighty in a moment, without a trial, because he already knows. Elihu ends with a hard verdict: Job speaks without knowledge, adds rebellion to his sin, and should be tested to the very end.
readings: Read as a defense of God's justice

Elihu's argument is about God's nature: the Creator and Sustainer of all cannot be unjust, or creation itself would fail. This is the strongest form of the friends' position, stated without accusing Job of particular crimes.
Read as a courtroom summing-up
Elihu acts like a prosecutor before a jury of sages: he reads Job's words into the record (34:5–6, 9), argues the law (34:10–30), and asks for a verdict (34:34–37). The reader is one of the jurors.

views.H: On a historical reading, the "wise men" are elders present at the scene, perhaps the men who once sat with Job at the gate (29:7–10).
views.C: Scholars note that 34:29–33 is among the most damaged passages in Job, and that the speech's addressee shifts between the group (34:2, 10, 34) and Job (34:16, 33). Some see this as evidence of a speech written for readers rather than for a scene.
views.W: Ancient Near Eastern wisdom often defends the gods' justice by appeal to their power and to the order of the world. The Babylonian Theodicy's friend argues that the gods' ways are far off. Elihu's argument from creation is similar in shape, but his God is one, and justice belongs to his nature, not only to his power.
views.J: Jewish readers hear in 34:10–12 the faith Abraham voiced, that the Judge of all the earth does right (Genesis 18:25). Gersonides (Ralbag) took Elihu's account of providence as the nearest to the truth of any human speaker in the book.
views.X: Christian readers hear in 34:19 the teaching that God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11), and in 34:14–15 the dependence of all life on God's spirit (Psalm 104:29–30). Many also note that Elihu's harsh verdict on Job (34:36–37) is not the LORD's (42:7).

deep.b:
The argument at its strongest. If God were unjust, nothing would hold the world together, for the same God who made it gives every creature its breath (34:13–15). Justice and rule go together: a ruler who hated justice could not govern (34:17). God's justice is impartial (34:19), all-seeing (34:21–22), and needs no trial because nothing is hidden from it (34:23). When he seems silent, no one can call him guilty, for his silence is not ignorance (34:29).

What Job might answer. Job never denied God's power; he complained that he saw power without justice (9:22–24; 24:1–12). Elihu's argument proves that God must be just, but not that Job is guilty. Elihu fills that gap with Job's own bold words (34:35–37). The LORD's later question to Job, "Would you even overturn my justice?" (40:8), shows that Elihu named a real danger; the LORD's verdict that Job spoke what is right about him (42:7) shows that Elihu's verdict on Job was not the last word.

echoes: 8:3; 12:11; 15:16; 27:2; Genesis 18:25; Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 104:29–30; Daniel 2:34; Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11; 40:8

settings.what: Elihu's second speech: God does no wrong
settings.to: "You wise men" and "you who know" (34:2), "you thoughtful men" (34:10): a circle of hearers, with asides to Job (34:16, 33)
settings.when: after his first speech, with Job still silent
settings.why: To ask the hearers to judge Job's words with him, to prove that God cannot be unjust, and to win their agreement that Job has spoken without knowledge.
settings.readers: If the book is from after the exile, as many think, its first readers had lost land, kings and Temple, and were tempted to Job's charge that God had denied them justice. Elihu's speech gives them the strongest case for God's justice; the book's ending asks them also to hear that honest complaint is not the same as rebellion.
views: "Wise men" may be the friends, addressed with irony after their failure (32:12).
Elders and sages of the community who have watched the debate (compare 29:7–10).
The speech asks the audience of the book to act as jury.

title: Does Goodness Matter to God?
sum: Elihu's third speech is short. He takes up Job's question: what do I gain by not sinning? He tells Job to look up at the clouds, so high above him. Human sin cannot hurt God, and human righteousness cannot help him. Both matter, but to other people.

Then he explains why so many cries go unanswered. People groan under oppression, but no one asks, "Where is God, who made me, who puts songs in the night?" They cry for relief, not for God, and pride keeps them from being heard. How much less, Elihu says, will God hear Job, who claims he cannot see God and is waiting for his case. Job opens his mouth for nothing.
readings: Read as a teaching on prayer
Elihu distinguishes between crying out from pain and seeking God himself (35:9–10). Songs in the night are the gift of someone who looks for the Maker, not only for rescue.
Read as a teaching on God's freedom
Because God is not helped or hurt by us, his justice is not self-interested. He does not reward goodness because he needs it.

views.H: Read as a scene, Elihu speaks to Job and to those who share his complaint, answering words Job had spoken earlier in the debate.
views.C: Scholars note that 35:5–8 closely follows Eliphaz (22:2–3, 12), and that the Old Greek lacked 35:3: it is asterisked in the hexaplaric witnesses and is still missing from Codex Vaticanus. The Old Greek also lacked 35:15–16. Verses 35:13–15 contain rare words whose meaning is uncertain.
views.W: The idea that the gods are untouched by human deeds is also found in some Mesopotamian and Greek thought. Elihu does not draw the conclusion that God is indifferent: righteousness matters, to people (35:8).
views.J: Jewish tradition loved the phrase "who puts songs in the night" (35:10); the Sabbath table songs are called zemirot, the same word.
views.X: Christian readers linked "songs in the night" with Paul and Silas singing in prison at midnight (Acts 16:25), and the warning about empty prayers with James 4:3. Some note that Job did seek God himself, so Elihu's diagnosis does not fit him.

deep.h: Is God too high to care?
deep.b: Elihu's argument (35:5–8) is easy to misread as "God does not care what you do." His point is narrower: God gains nothing from our goodness and loses nothing from our sin, so he cannot be bribed by the righteous or wounded by the wicked. Righteousness and wickedness still matter, because they reach other people (35:8). The danger of the argument is that it can make God seem distant, which is exactly what Job has complained about (23:3, 8–9). The LORD's speeches will answer differently: God is high above Job, yet he comes near enough to speak (38:1).

settings.what: Elihu's third speech: why the cries go unanswered
settings.to: Job, "and your friends along with you" (35:4)
settings.when: after his second speech, still without a reply from Job
settings.why: To answer Job's question about what goodness gains, and to explain why God seems silent: the cries he does not answer are empty cries for relief, made in pride, without seeking God.
settings.readers: First readers who prayed and seemed unheard, perhaps under foreign rule if the book is from after the exile, as many think, are invited to ask whether they are seeking God himself or only relief. The book also lets them notice that Job, who did seek God, is not described fairly here.
views: "Your friends" are Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, who share in the failed debate.
Anyone who agrees with Job, including the readers.

title: Rescued Through Suffering
sum: Elihu asks for a little more patience: there is still more to say on God's behalf. He sets out his clearest teaching. God is mighty but despises no one. He does not keep the wicked alive, and he never takes his eyes off the righteous. If the righteous are bound in chains of affliction, God shows them their sins and opens their ears to discipline. If they listen, they live out their days in good things; if not, they cross the River and die without knowledge. God rescues the afflicted through their affliction.

Elihu turns to warn Job: God was drawing him toward a wide place and a full table, but Job is consumed by the fate of the wicked. Then the speech rises into a hymn. God is lifted high in power; what teacher is like him? He draws up the water drop by drop, spreads the clouds, sends lightning and thunder from his pavilion, and with the same rain both judges nations and feeds them.
readings: Read as a theology of suffering

Suffering can be a classroom: God uses pain to open the ear of the one who would not hear (36:10, 15). This is the strongest version of the idea in the book, and it has shaped Jewish and Christian thought ever since.
Read as a prelude to the storm
From 36:22 Elihu's words turn from Job to God, and from argument to praise. The rain and thunder he describes lead straight into the storm of 37:1–5 and the voice of 38:1.

views.H: Read as a scene, Elihu may be watching clouds gather as he speaks; his description moves from the first drops to the thunder.
views.C: 36:16–21 is one of the most corrupt passages in Job, and the Greek differs widely; much of the Greek of 36:5–11, 36:16, 36:20–21 and 36:24–37:5 is Theodotion's, filling gaps in the Old Greek. Scholars note that Elihu's hymn on rain and storm (36:26–37:13) anticipates the LORD's own questions about the weather (38:22–30, 34–38).
views.W: Storm hymns are common in the ancient Near East: Baal's thunder in Ugaritic poems, Adad's in Mesopotamian ones. Like Psalm 29, Elihu's hymn gives the storm to the one God.
views.J: Jewish tradition developed the idea of yissurin shel ahavah, "sufferings of love," which God sends to the righteous to purify and reward them (Berakhot 5a, which builds on Proverbs 3:12 and Isaiah 53:10); Elihu's "rescued through affliction" (36:15) expresses a similar idea. Gersonides read Elihu's teaching as close to the book's own view of providence.
views.X: Christians link 36:15 with Paul's "suffering produces endurance" (Romans 5:3–4) and Hebrews 12:5–11, where God disciplines those he loves. Traditions differ over whether God sends sickness to teach (see "Where Christians differ").

deep.h: Discipline: the view at its strongest, and its limits
deep.b:
Elihu's teaching in 36:8–15 is that God allows the righteous to fall into trouble so that they will see their faults and turn back; those who listen are restored, and those who refuse die "without knowledge." At its strongest, this gives suffering meaning without making it a simple punishment, and it holds out real hope. Many sufferers have found it true in their own lives (Psalm 119:67, 71).

Its limit is the case of Job himself. The prologue says Job's suffering was not sent to correct a fault (1:8; 2:3), and the LORD never tells Job that it was. The book does not reject Elihu's teaching, but it refuses to let it explain all suffering.

Elihu's last speech ends in a hymn that follows the year's weather: autumn rains (36:27–33), the thunderstorm (37:1–5), winter snow and ice (37:6–13), and the hot, still days of summer under a bronze sky (37:17–18), until a golden light appears from the north (37:22). Many readers think the hymn is meant to sound like a real storm coming closer. Its questions to Job (37:14–20) prepare for the LORD's questions in chapters 38–41.

traditions.q: Does God send suffering and sickness to correct and teach people, as Elihu says (33:19–30; 36:8–15)?
views: Suffering is not always a punishment for sin, but God can use it for conversion and growth, and united with Christ's suffering it can share in the work of redemption (John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris 12, 19, 24; compare Colossians 1:24).

God in his providence sometimes leaves his own children to trials and afflictions to correct them for former sins, to humble them, and to make them more watchful and dependent on him; for believers such affliction is a father's discipline, not a penalty (Westminster Confession 5.5).

Healing is provided for in Christ's atonement and is the privilege of all believers (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, article 12). Many Pentecostal teachers deny that God wills sickness as a teaching tool and urge prayer for healing; others in the movement accept that God may allow suffering for a purpose. The tradition is divided on how far.

settings.what: Elihu's fourth speech: discipline, and the God of the storm
settings.to: Job (36:2, 16–21; 37:14–20), with all the hearers called to listen to the thunder (37:2, plural)
settings.when: his last speech, ending as a storm gathers; the LORD answers Job from the windstorm right after (38:1)
settings.why: To give his clearest teaching (God rescues the afflicted through their affliction), to warn Job not to turn to evil, and to lead Job and the hearers from argument to awe at God's power in the storm.
settings.readers: If the book is from after the exile, as many think, first readers who saw the exile as God's discipline could hear Elihu's teaching as a word of hope: chains can be a classroom, and those who listen can be restored. The hymn's turn to the storm prepares them, as it prepares Job, to hear God speak for himself.
views: The speech is built to introduce the LORD's speeches, ending where they begin, in the storm.
Elihu tries to say what only God can say, and God's arrival silences him.

title: The Storm Arrives
sum: At the thunder Elihu's heart pounds. He calls everyone to listen to the roar of God's voice as lightning flashes to the ends of the earth. God commands the snow and the rain; work stops and the animals take cover; the storm wind comes from its chamber, and God's breath freezes the waters. The clouds go wherever he sends them, for punishment or for his land or for loyal love.

Then Elihu turns to Job one last time. Stand still and consider God's wonders. Do you know how he balances the clouds? Can you hammer out the sky like a metal mirror? Who would dare ask to speak with him? No one can look at the light when the clouds clear; from the north comes golden splendor. The Almighty is beyond our reach, great in power and justice. And then, out of the storm, the LORD answers Job (38:1).
readings: Read as the herald of God's speech
Elihu's storm becomes God's storm. His questions anticipate God's, and his last line, that God is beyond our reach, is overturned at once when God speaks.
Read as the end of human answers
Elihu, the last and most confident human speaker, ends by admitting that "because of the dark, we cannot lay out our case" (37:19). Even he falls silent before the storm.

views.H: On a historical reading, a real storm broke over the scene as Elihu finished, and God spoke to Job out of it.
views.C: Scholars who think Elihu was added later point out how closely 37:14–18 anticipates 38–39; scholars who think he is original point to the same closeness as deliberate design. The text of 37:7, 9, 13 and 22–24 has several uncertain words.
views.W: The north (tsafon) was the home of Baal in Ugaritic poems, and storm and golden splendor belong to the storm god's appearing. Israel's poets used such language for the LORD's glory (Psalm 48:2; Ezekiel 1:4) without taking over the myth.
views.J: The Talmud reads 37:7, "he seals the hand of every person," as the moment at death when a person signs the record of his own deeds (Ta'anit 11a).
views.X: Christian readers see in Elihu's awe before the storm a preparation for meeting God, and some compare him with John the Baptist, who announced the one coming after him. Others note that God's coming makes even Elihu's best words unnecessary.

deep.b: Elihu's last words lead straight into God's. He describes the storm (37:1–5); God speaks from the storm (38:1). He asks "Do you know...?" about the clouds (37:15–16); God asks "Do you know...?" about the mountain goats and the laws of the heavens (38:33; 39:1). He talks of snow, rain and ice (37:6–10); God asks whether Job has seen the storehouses of the snow (38:22) and who gave birth to the ice (38:29). The differences are just as striking. Elihu talks about God; God talks to Job. Elihu draws a lesson about Job's guilt; God draws none. Elihu says the Almighty is beyond reach (37:23); God comes.

The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking rightly about him (42:7–9), but says nothing about Elihu. Readers explain the silence four ways. He was added later, so the ending never knew him. He spoke rightly, so needed no rebuke. He was beneath notice, a young man whose words God simply passes over. His words were answered by God's, who takes up his themes (the storm, the questions) and drops his accusations. The book does not decide for us.
